Benchmark.title: CIS Tencent Cloud Enterprise Foundation Benchmark
Benchmark.description: All CIS Benchmarks ™ (Benchmarks) focus on technical configuration settings used to maintain and/or increase the security of the addressed technology, and they should be used in conjunction with other essential cyber hygiene tasks like: • Monitoring the base operating system and applications for vulnerabilities and quickly updating with the latest security patches. • End-point protection (Antivirus software, Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), etc.). • Logging and monitoring user and system activity. In the end, the Benchmarks are designed to be a key component of a comprehensive cybersecurity program. Important Usage Information All Benchmarks are available free for non-commercial use from the CIS Website. They can be used to manually assess and remediate systems and applications. In lieu of manual assessment and remediation, there are several tools available to assist with assessment: • CIS Configuration Assessment Tool (CIS-CAT ® Pro Assessor) • CIS Benchmarks ™ Certified 3rd Party Tooling These tools make the hardening process much more scalable for large numbers of systems and applications. NOTE: Some tooling focuses only on the Benchmark Recommendations that can be fully automated (skipping ones marked Manual). It is important that ALL Recommendations ( Automated and Manual) be addressed since all are important for properly securing systems and are typically in scope for audits. Key Stakeholders Cybersecurity is a collaborative effort, and cross functional cooperation is imperative within an organization to discuss, test, and deploy Benchmarks in an effective and efficient way. The Benchmarks are developed to be best practice configuration guidelines applicable to a wide range of use cases. In some organizations, exceptions to specific Recommendations will be needed, and this team should work to prioritize the problematic Recommendations based on several factors like risk, time, cost, and labor. These exceptions should be properly categorized and documented for auditing purposes. Apply the Correct Version of a Benchmark Benchmarks are developed and tested for a specific set of products and versions and applying an incorrect Benchmark to a system can cause the resulting pass/fail score to be incorrect. This is due to the assessment of settings that do not apply to the target systems. To assure the correct Benchmark is being assessed: • Deploy the Benchmark applicable to the way settings are managed in the environment: An example of this is the Microsoft Windows family of Benchmarks, which have separate Benchmarks for Group Policy, Intune, and Stand-alone systems based upon how system management is deployed. Applying the wrong Benchmark in this case will give invalid results. • Use the most recent version of a Benchmark: This is true for all Benchmarks, but especially true for cloud technologies. Cloud technologies change frequently and using an older version of a Benchmark may have invalid methods for auditing and remediation. Exceptions The guidance items in the Benchmarks are called recommendations and not requirements, and exceptions to some of them are expected and acceptable. The Benchmarks strive to be a secure baseline, or starting point, for a specific technology, with known issues identified during Benchmark development are documented in the Impact section of each Recommendation. In addition, organizational, system specific requirements, or local site policy may require changes as well, or an exception to a Recommendation or group of Recommendations (e.g. A Benchmark could Recommend that a Web server not be installed on the system, but if a system's primary purpose is to function as a Webserver, there should be a documented exception to this Recommendation for that specific server). In the end, exceptions to some Benchmark Recommendations are common and acceptable, and should be handled as follows: • The reasons for the exception should be reviewed cross-functionally and be well documented for audit purposes. • A plan should be developed for mitigating, or eliminating, the exception in the future, if applicable. • If the organization decides to accept the risk of this exception (not work toward mitigation or elimination), this should be documented for audit purposes. It is the responsibility of the organization to determine their overall security policy, and which settings are applicable to their unique needs based on the overall risk profile for the organization. Remediation CIS has developed Build Kits for many technologies to assist in the automation of hardening systems. Build Kits are designed to correspond to Benchmark's “Remediation” section, which provides the manual remediation steps necessary to make that Recommendation compliant to the Benchmark. When remediating systems (changing configuration settings on deployed systems as per the Benchmark's Recommendations), please approach this with caution and test thoroughly. The following is a reasonable remediation approach to follow: • CIS Build Kits, or internally developed remediation methods should never be applied to production systems without proper testing. • Proper testing consists of the following: o Understand the configuration (including installed applications) of the targeted systems. Various parts of the organization may need different configurations (e.g., software developers vs standard office workers). o Read the Impact section of the given Recommendation to help determine if there might be an issue with the targeted systems. o Test the configuration changes with representative lab system(s). If issues arise during testing, they can be resolved prior to deploying to any production systems. o When testing is complete, initially deploy to a small sub-set of production systems and monitor closely for issues. If there are issues, they can be resolved prior to deploying more broadly. o When the initial deployment above is completes successfully, iteratively deploy to additional systems and monitor closely for issues. Repeat this process until the full deployment is complete. Summary Using the Benchmarks Certified tools, working as a team with key stakeholders, being selective with exceptions, and being careful with remediation deployment, it is possible to harden large numbers of deployed systems in a cost effective, efficient, and safe manner. NOTE: As previously stated, the PDF versions of the CIS Benchmarks ™ are available for free, non-commercial use on the CIS Website. All other formats of the CIS Benchmarks ™ (MS Word, Excel, and Build Kits) are available for CIS SecureSuite ® members. CIS-CAT ® Pro is also available to CIS SecureSuite ® members. Target Technology Details This security configuration benchmark covers the fundamental elements of Tencent Cloud Enterprise (TCE) and provides guidance on security option configurations for certain TCE services, focusing on fundamental, testable, and architecture-agnostic settings. The specific TCE services in scope for this document include: • Kubernetes Engine (TKE) • Cloud Virtual Machine (CVM) • Cloud Object Storage (COS) • Cloud Block Storage (CBS) • Cloud File Storage (CFS) • TDSQL for MySQL • MariaDB (MariaDB) • TDSQL for PostgreSQL • Application Operations Platform • CloudAudit • Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWP) • Backup Recovery Management System (BRMS) • Cloud Access Management (CAM) • TDMQ for CKafka (CKafka) • Cloud Load Balancer (CLB) • Cloud Storage Private (CSP) • Disaster Recovery Management System (DRMS) • Distributed Transaction Framework (DTF) • TDMQ for Apache Pulsar (TDMQ Pulsar) • TDMQ for RabbitMQ (TDMQ RabbitMQ) • CloudDB for Redis® (Redis®) • TDMQ for Apache RocketMQ (TDMQ RocketMQ) • Security Group • Cloud Task (TCT) • Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)

Rule.title: Ensure that Image Repositories Are Configured with Appropriate Permissions
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Repositories can be public or private. Public repositories allow all users on the internet to access and download images. If an image contains sensitive information, you are advised to configure the repository as private to prevent information leakage.

Rationale:
Images in public repositories that contain sensitive information (such as keys or user data) are directly exposed to the internet, allowing attackers to easily access the data.
Restricting such repositories to private reduces the risk of unauthorized access and information leakage.</VulnDiscussion>

Enabling the Image Repository (if not already enabled) 1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Kubernetes Engine.
2. In the left navigation pane, choose Image Repository > My Images.

4. On the Image Details tab, set Type to Private, and click OK to save the change.

3. On the Image List tab, review the Type field for each repository and verify that all repositories which store images containing or likely to contain sensitive information are configured as Private.

Rule.title: Ensure that TKE Clusters Are Bound to Security Groups with Least-Privilege Rules
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that each TKE cluster is bound to an appropriate security group and that the security group rules enforce the principle of least privilege for network access to the cluster.

Rationale:
If TKE clusters are associated with overly permissive security group rules (for example, allowing unrestricted inbound access), the attack surface of the cluster is significantly increased. Binding clusters to security groups with minimal, business-justified ingress and egress rules helps ensure that only authorized IP addresses and services can access the cluster control plane and worker nodes, thereby reducing the risk of unauthorized access and compromise.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Tencent Cloud Enterprise Foundation Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Adjusting Security Group Rules for Existing Clusters 1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Kubernetes Engine.
2. Select the target cluster and identify the bound security group.
3. Navigate to the security group management page, and review and update the rules to:
• Restrict source IP ranges to trusted IPs or networks.
• Restrict open ports to only those required by the cluster and applications.
• Remove any unnecessary or overly broad rules (for example, public exposure where not required).

check.check-content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Kubernetes Engine.
2. Go to Cluster, click the cluster ID you want to review, and verify that a security group is associated with the cluster.
3. Review the inbound and outbound rules of the associated security group on the cloud firewall / security group management page and verify that:
• Only required IP ranges and ports (based on business and operational needs) are allowed to access the cluster.
• Unnecessary broad rules (for example, 0.0.0.0/0 for sensitive ports) are not present.
4. Optionally, validate that the IP addresses not permitted by the security group rules cannot access the cluster endpoints.

Rule.title: Ensure that CLB Instances Are Bound to Security Groups with Least-Privilege Rules
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that each CLB instance is bound to an appropriate security group and that the security group rules enforce the principle of least privilege, for example, restricting inbound access on service ports to trusted IP address ranges.

Rationale:
Security groups function as virtual firewalls for CLB instances. If CLB instances are associated with overly permissive rules (such as allowing 0.0.0.0/0 where restriction is expected), the instances are exposed to potential attacks from any internet source.
Binding CLB instances to security groups with minimal, business-justified ingress rules and trusted IP allowlists reduces exposure to malicious traffic and lowers the risk of unauthorized access and compromise.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Load Balancer.

4. Click Bind, select an appropriate security group, and click OK.

• Limit open ports to those strictly required by the services behind the CLB.
• Remove any unnecessary or overly broad rules, especially the rules allowing 0.0.0.0/0 where not strictly required by design.

check.check-content:

2. Go to LB Instance List, locate the target CLB instance, and click More to open the details page.
3. Click Configure Security Group and verify that:
• The CLB instance is bound to at least one security group.
• The bound security group does not allow unrestricted access from source IP 0.0.0.0/0 on ports that should be restricted to trusted IP ranges and are only limited to business-justified IP ranges and ports.

Rule.title: Ensure that Least-Privilege Policies Are Configured for COS Buckets
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that bucket policies for COS buckets are configured according to the principle of least privilege. Buckets must not be configured to allow unrestricted read access (for example, read access for any user on the internet), as this can expose object names and data to unauthorized parties.

Rationale:
Bucket policies control which users or services can access a COS bucket and its contents, and what operations they can perform. If a bucket policy grants broad read access (such as anonymous or public read), attackers can:
• List object names (traversal of file names).
• Download files directly.
• Access sensitive information stored in the bucket.
Configuring bucket policies with minimal, business-justified permissions reduces the risk of unauthorized access and sensitive data leakage.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Object Storage.
2. Go to Bucket List, locate the target bucket, then click the bucket name or Configuration Management to enter the configuration management page.
3. Click Permission Management > Policy Permission Settings.
4. Click Graphic Settings > Add Policy.
5. Review and configure the policy to:
• Grant access only to specific, authorized accounts, roles, or services.
• Avoid any statements that allow public or anonymous read access.
• Limit allowed actions to those strictly required.

check.check-content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Object Storage.
2. Go to Bucket List, locate the bucket to be reviewed, and click the bucket name or Configuration Management to enter the configuration management page.
3. Go to Permission Management > Policy Permission Settings, and review the configured bucket policy. Verify that:
• Access is restricted to specific, authorized users, roles, and/or services.
• There is no policy granting public or anonymous read access.
• Permissions granted are limited to the minimum required (least privilege).

Rule.title: Ensure that Hotlink Protection Is Enabled for COS Buckets
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that hotlink protection is enabled for COS buckets that are accessed over the public network. Configure hotlink protection with an appropriate allowlist (and optional blocklist) so that only trusted domains or IP addresses can directly reference COS resources.

Rationale:
Enabling hotlink protection and restricting access to a controlled set of allowed domains or IPs helps prevent malicious traffic consumption and reduces the risk of financial loss.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Object Storage.
2. Go to Bucket List, locate the target bucket, and click the bucket name or Configuration Management to enter the configuration management page.
3. Go to Security Management > Hotlink Protection Settings to enter the Hotlink Protection Settings page.
4. Click Modify, and toggle Current Status to On to enable the hotlink protection.
5. Configure the following:
• Set Type to Whitelist.
• Set Allow Empty Referer to Deny (unless there are justified business requirements).
• Enter the trusted domain names or IP addresses that are permitted to reference bucket resources.
6. Click Save.

check.check-content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Object Storage.
2. Go to Bucket List, locate the bucket you want to review, and click the bucket name or Configuration Management at the end of the bucket to enter the configuration management page.
3. Go to Security Management > Hotlink Protection Settings and verify that:
• The hotlink protection feature is enabled.
• A Whitelist is configured with the trusted domain names or IP addresses that are allowed to reference the bucket resources.
• Allow Empty Referer is set according to the least privilege principle (typically Denied for internet-facing bucket).

Rule.title: Ensure that Logging Is Enabled for COS Buckets
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that logging is enabled for COS buckets. Configure the log management feature so that detailed access logs for a source bucket are written to a designated destination bucket in the same region.

Rationale:
COS bucket logging records detailed access information (for example, requester, accessed object, time, and operation type) and stores it as log files in a specified destination bucket. Enabling logging:
• Provides traceability for access to sensitive data;
• Supports investigation of abnormal or suspicious access patterns;
• Aids in incident response and forensic analysis;
• Improves operational visibility and compliance reporting.
Without logging, it is difficult to detect or investigate unauthorized access or misuse of COS resources.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that Cloud Workload Protection Platform Is Installed on All CVM Instances
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that the Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWP) agent is installed and running on all CVM instances. CWP provides security capabilities such as Trojan detection and removal, password cracking interception, login behavior audit, vulnerability management, and asset component identification. Failure to install the CWP agent will expose CVM instances to network security threats and increase the risk of data leakage.

Rationale:
CWP provides continuous, real-time monitoring of the security status of CVM instances, helping to protect against network attacks and enhancing overall host security. Without the CWP agent, it is more difficult to detect attacks, abnormal activities, and vulnerabilities on CVM instances, increasing the likelihood of data compromise.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to CWP.
2. In the left navigation pane, go to Asset Management > Server List.
3. Click Install CWP Agent for the target CVM instance to view the installation instructions.
4. After installation, verify on the target CVM instance that both YDService and YDLive processes are running.

check.check-content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to CWP.
2. In the left navigation pane, choose Asset Management > Server List to enter the Server List page.
3. Select All Servers and verify that all CVM hosts are shown as protected by CWP.
4. On each CVM host, execute the following command to verify the CWP agent is running normally:
• Execute the command
ps -ef | grep YD
• and verify that both YDService and YDLive processes are running.

Rule.title: Ensure that SSH Key-based Authentication Is Used for Linux CVM Login
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that SSH key-based authentication is used for logging in to Linux CVM instances instead of traditional password authentication. SSH key authentication is more secure and convenient, and helps prevent unauthorized access caused by weak or compromised passwords. (Only applicable for Linux machines)

Rationale:
SSH key-based login provides stronger authentication than password-based login and is resistant to brute-force attacks. By eliminating the need to enter a password during login and relying on cryptographic key pairs, the risk of credential guessing and credential stuffing is significantly reduced, thereby enhancing the overall security of CVM instances.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Creating SSH Keys 1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Virtual Machine.
2. In the left navigation pane, click SSH Key.
3. Select Create Key.
4. Choose one of the following methods:
• Create Key Pair: Enter the key name and click Confirm.
• Use an existing public key: Enter the key name and paste the existing public key, then click Confirm.
5. In the pop-up window, click Download to download the private key. Download must be completed within 10 minutes. Store the private key securely.
Binding Keys to CVM Instances/Unbinding Keys from CVM Instances 1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Virtual Machine.
2. In the left navigation pane, go to SSH Key.
3. Select an SSH key and click Bind/Unbind CVM.
4. Select a region, then:
• For binding, select the CVM instances to which the SSH key should be bound.
• For unbinding, deselect (cancel) the CVM instances from the list on the right.
5. Click Confirm.
6. Wait for the delivery of the SSH key to complete, and verify the prompt indicating whether the operation completed successfully.

check.check-content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Virtual Machine.
2. Go to Instances and identify the Linux CVM instances that require SSH access.
3. Verify that an SSH key is associated with the instance (for example, on the instance details page under Login Information or SSH Key).
4. From an administrator workstation, attempt to log in to a target Linux CVM instance using SSH key authentication:
• Run
ssh -i <private_key_file_path> <user>@<host>
• Verify that login using the SSH key is successful.

Rule.title: Ensure that CVM Instances Are Bound to Security Groups with Least-Privilege Rules
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that each CVM instance is bound to an appropriate security group and that the security group rules are configured based on the principle of least privilege. Trusted IP ranges should be explicitly allowed for required service ports to ensure secure access, and unnecessary or broad access must be avoided.

Rationale:
Security groups act as virtual firewalls that control network traffic to and from CVM instances. Configuring security group rules according to the principle of least privilege can reduce exposure to malicious or unauthorized IP addresses, lowering the risk of network attacks and unauthorized access to hosts.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Creating a Security Group 1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Virtual Machine.
2. In the left navigation pane, go to Security Group.
3. Click Create, then select Custom for Template, enter a security group name, and click OK.
4. Click Set Rule Now and configure rules as follows:
• Add policies to deny access from all IP address to all ports by default.
• Add allow rules for trusted IP address ranges and required service ports based on business needs.
Binding an Instance to a Security Group 1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Virtual Machine.
2. In the left navigation pane, go to Instances, then click the ID or name of a CVM instance to enter the instance details page.
3. On the instance details page, click More > Configure Security Group in the upper-right corner.
4. In the pop-up window, select the new security group name(s) (multiple selections are allowed), and click Confirm.

check.check-content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Cloud Virtual Machine.
2. On the Instances page, click the ID or name of the target CVM instance to enter the instance details page.
3. On the instance details page, click More > Configure Security Group in the upper-right corner to verify that the CVM instance is bound to at least one security group.
4. Review the rules of the bound security group(s) and verify that:
• Only trusted IP address ranges are allowed to access required service ports.
• Unnecessary or overly broad rules (e.g. wide-open access to all ports or 0.0.0.0/0 where it is not required) are not configured.

Rule.title: Ensure that Intrusion Prevention Policies Are Configured and Enabled in Cloud Workload Protection Platform
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that intrusion prevention policies are configured and enabled in CWP, including file (virus/Trojan) scanning rules and network attack detection rules. Proper configuration helps detect and block malicious files and network attacks on protected hosts in a timely manner.

Rationale:
Intrusion prevention policies in CWP provide file-based and network-based protection by scanning for malicious files (such as Trojans and viruses), monitoring critical paths in real time, and detecting attempted network attacks. Correctly configured and enabled policies improve the ability to identify and respond to security threats early, reducing the risk of compromise and lateral movement within the environment.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Tencent Cloud Enterprise Foundation Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to CWP.
2. Go to Intrusion Defense, and configure file/virus scanning policies as follows:
• A scheduled scanning policy is created and enabled to ensure timely detection of Trojan virus files on hosts.
• The real-time monitoring switch is turned on to monitor malicious files in critical paths.
• (Recommended) Automatic isolation is enabled to automatically isolate detected malicious files.
• Network attack detection policies are configured.
• The Attempted Attack Detection switch is turned on.

1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to CWP.

Rule.title: Ensure that Scheduled Vulnerability Scanning Is Configured and Enabled in Cloud Workload Protection Platform
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that scheduled vulnerability scanning policies are configured and enabled in CWP. Properly configured policies allow hosts to be scanned at regular intervals so that security vulnerabilities can be identified and addressed in a timely manner.

Rationale:
Scheduled vulnerability scanning helps detect known vulnerabilities in operating systems, middleware, and applications before they can be exploited. Enabling regular scanning and vulnerability protection improves visibility into the security posture of hosts, supports timely remediation, and reduces the risk of compromise due to unpatched vulnerabilities.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that Security Baseline Check Policies Are Configured and Enabled in Cloud Workload Protection Platform
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that security baseline check policies are configured and enabled in CWP.
Security baseline checks evaluate host configuration against defined baseline requirements and help identify configuration compliance issues in a timely manner.

Rationale:
Security baseline check policies provide continuous visibility into whether hosts comply with defined security configuration standards (for example, system hardening, service configuration, and account policies). Enabling and properly configuring these policies helps detect deviations from the required baseline early, supports remediation, and reduces the risk of compromise caused by insecure configurations.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that Security Groups Are Configured with Least- Privilege Rules for CVM Instances
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that security groups are created and used to control network access to CVM instances. Security group rules must be configured based on the principle of least privilege so that only trusted IP address ranges and required ports are allowed, reducing unnecessary exposure of CVM assets.

Rationale:
Security groups act as virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic to CVM instances. Configuring allowlist-based security group policies according to the principle of least privilege limits access to trusted sources and required services only, thereby reducing the risk of network attacks and unauthorized access to CVM instances.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that API Keys Are Not Enabled for High-privilege Sub- accounts
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that high-privilege sub-accounts (for example, sub-accounts with super administrator-level permissions) do not have active API keys. API keys are used for programmatic access and are often stored in codes, scripts, or configuration files, making them prone to leakage. If a high-privilege API key is compromised, an attacker may gain control over a wide range of cloud resources.

Rationale:
Disabling API keys for high-privilege sub-accounts reduces the risk that leaked or stolen keys can be used to take over or manipulate critical cloud assets. Restricting programmatic access for such accounts supports the principle of least privilege and simplifies management and control of high-risk identities.</VulnDiscussion>

5. For each existing API key associated with the high-privilege sub-account:
• Disable the API key, or
• Delete the API key, if programmatic access is not required.
6. If programmatic access is required, consider:
• Using lower-privilege service or automation accounts with scoped permissions.
• Applying key rotation and strong lifecycle management controls to those lower-privilege accounts.

Rule.title: Ensure that Sub-account Passwords Expire Within 365 Days or Less
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that sub-account password policies enforce periodic password changes. Sub- account passwords are primary credentials for interactive access. If passwords are not changed for extended periods (for example, more than 365 days), the risk of password compromise and long-term unauthorized use increases.

Rationale:
Regularly updating sub-account passwords reduces the likelihood that compromised credentials can be used for extended periods. Enforcing a maximum password validity period (for example, 365 days or less), combined with appropriate password complexity and reuse restrictions, strengthens overall account security and limits the impact of credential exposure.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Log in to the tenant console and navigate to Account Center.
2. Go to Cloud Access Management > User Management > User Settings to enter the security settings page.
3. In the Password Rule Setting module, click Modify to modify the password policy, including:
• Include At Least: Require the password to contain at least two of the following character types: uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits, or special characters. (By default, uppercase and lowercase letters are mandatory.)
• Minimum Password Length: Set the minimum password length. The recommended value is 14 characters at least. (Default is 10 characters, maximum is 32 characters.)
• Password Period: Set the password validity period to 365 days or less (a value of 0 indicates no restriction; the maximum configurable value is 365 days).
• Repeated Limit: Configure password reuse restrictions (default is 1, maximum is 24) to prevent reuse of recent passwords. The recommended repetition is 5 times or more.
• Password Blacklist: Configure a blacklist of disallowed strings (up to 10 entries) to prevent use of easily guessed or sensitive terms.
4. Click Confirm to save the password rule settings. After these settings take effect, sub-account passwords must be reset upon expiration, calculated from the last password change.

Rule.title: Ensure that Sub-accounts Do Not Have Both Programmatic and Console Access Enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that sub-accounts are not granted both programmatic access (API keys) and user interface (console) access at the same time, unless there is a clearly justified business need. Simultaneously enabling both access methods expands the account’s attack surface and can blur the distinction between human users and machine/automation accounts, increasing the risk of misuse if credentials are compromised.

Rationale:
Allowing both API key access and console password access for the same sub-account increases the scope of permissions that can be abused if any credential is leaked or stolen. Separating machine access (API keys) and human access (console) into different accounts and limiting each sub-account to a single access method reduces the impact of credential compromise and supports better access governance and least privilege.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that No API Keys Are Enabled for Root Accounts
Rule.description:

Root accounts typically have full administrative permissions over all resources under the account, and API keys provide programmatic access that is often embedded in code, scripts, or configuration files, making them prone to leakage. If a root account API key is compromised, an attacker could gain extensive control over cloud assets.

Rationale:
Disabling API keys for root accounts reduces the risk that leaked or stolen keys can be used to take over or manipulate critical cloud resources. Restricting programmatic access for the root account limits the potential impact of credential compromise and supports the principle of least privilege by encouraging the use of lower-privilege identities for automation.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that MFA Is Enabled for Sub-account Operation Protection
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that sub-accounts are bound to an MFA device and that Operation Protection is configured to require MFA verification for sensitive operations. Without MFA binding, sub-accounts cannot use MFA for secondary verification during critical operations, increasing the risk of unauthorized or high-impact changes.

Rationale:
Requiring MFA for operation protection adds a strong second factor for high-risk actions (such as security configuration changes, permission modifications, or asset deletions).
This reduces the likelihood of accidental or incorrect operations and raises the attack threshold for attackers, thereby limiting the potential impact of destructive actions.</VulnDiscussion>

Leaving such unused API keys enabled unnecessarily expands the attack surface and may provide attackers with additional entry points if the keys are exposed.

Rationale:
Deleting API keys for accounts that have never logged in and are not actively used reduces the risk of data leakage, resource abuse, or unauthorized operations performed via compromised credentials. Removing unused keys is a key part of good credential hygiene and supports the principle of least privilege.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that API Keys Unused for a Defined Period Are Removed from Sub-accounts

Rationale:
Deleting deprecated API keys for sub-accounts reduces the risk of data leakage, resource abuse, or unauthorized operations performed with credentials that are no longer required for business activities. Regular cleanup of unused keys improves overall credential hygiene and supports the principle of least privilege.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that Sub-account API Keys Are Rotated Every 90 Days or Less
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that sub-account API keys (AK/SK) are rotated regularly (for example, at least every 90 days). Sub-account API keys are primary credentials for programmatic access.
If keys are not changed for an extended period, the likelihood and impact of key compromise increase.

Rationale:
Periodic rotation of sub-account API keys reduces the window of opportunity for attackers to exploit exposed or leaked credentials. Regular key updates help mitigate risks such as data leakage, resource abuse, and unauthorized operations, and form an important part of secure credential lifecycle management.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that Login Protection Is Enabled for Root Accounts
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that login protection (multi-factor authentication or equivalent) is enabled for root accounts. The root account typically has full administrative permissions over all resources under the account. If a root account is compromised, all associated cloud assets are at very high risk. Enabling login protection adds a second step to the login process and reduces the likelihood of successful malicious logins.

Rationale:
Enabling multi-factor authentication (MFA) for root account login significantly reduces the risk of account takeover. Even if the password is compromised, an attacker cannot gain access without the second factor (for example, MFA device or SMS code). This additional verification step blocks the vast majority of automated and credential-based attacks against high-privilege accounts.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that No More Than One Active Access Key Exists per Sub-account

<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that each sub-account has no more than one active API key (AK/SK).
Maintaining multiple API keys for the same sub-account increases the credential exposure surface and complicates management. If any of these keys are leaked, attackers gain additional opportunities to abuse programmatic access.

Rationale:
Limiting each sub-account to a single API key (or none, where not required) reduces the risk of key leakage, simplifies key lifecycle management, and improves traceability of API usage. Fewer active keys per identity aligns with the principle of least privilege and helps contain potential compromise.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that MFA Is Enabled for Root Account Operation Protection

<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enabled for operation protection on the root account. The root account typically has full administrative privileges over all resources under the account. If a root account is misused — either through human error or malicious compromise — critical cloud assets may be affected. Enabling MFA for sensitive operations adds an extra verification step beyond username and password, reducing the likelihood and impact of unauthorized or erroneous changes.

Rationale:
Operation protection with MFA helps prevent high-risk actions from being performed without additional verification. This reduces the probability of unintentional configuration changes and raises the difficulty for attackers attempting destructive operations, thereby enhancing the overall security of the root account and associated resources.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that Sub-accounts Unused for 45 Days or Longer Are Disabled

<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that sub-accounts which have been inactive for an extended period (for example, 45 days or more) and are no longer required are identified and deleted.
Deprecated or unused sub-accounts may still retain permissions and credentials, increasing the risk of unauthorized access, asset unavailability, or data breaches if they are abused by former users or attackers.

Rationale:
Deleting deprecated sub-accounts reduces the risk of misuse of residual credentials (such as passwords or API keys) and limits the number of identities with access to cloud resources. This supports the principle of least privilege, simplifies identity lifecycle management, and improves overall account security.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that CAM Policies Comply with the Principle of Least Privilege
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that sub-accounts are granted only the minimum permissions required to perform their duties. Assigning excessive or high-level permissions to sub-accounts significantly increases security risk; if such an account is compromised, an attacker may gain broad control over cloud resources and sensitive data.

Rationale:
Applying the principle of least privilege limits each sub-account to only the actions and resources necessary for its role. This reduces the likelihood of sensitive data exposure, unauthorized changes, and abuse of elevated privileges, whether due to compromise or incorrect use.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that CLB Instances Are Configured with Health Checks and Proactively Monitored

Rationale:
Ensure normal CLB health checks and status metrics to reduce the risk of undetected production service failures. Regularly identifying and troubleshooting abnormal CLB instances helps prevent traffic interruption, misrouting of requests, and service degradation.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that CLB Does Not Forward High-Risk Ports
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that Cloud Load Balancer (CLB) instances do not expose high-risk management or internal service ports to the public network. CLB listeners should only forward required public service ports (for example, 80 and 443), and must not forward administrative or internal ports (for example, SSH, RDP, and database ports) directly to the internet.

Rationale:
Blocking high-risk port forwarding on CLBs reduces the exposure of internal management and sensitive services to the public network. This lowers the likelihood of malicious scanning, brute-force attacks, and exploitation attempts against management interfaces or backend services, and supports the principle of minimal service exposure.</VulnDiscussion>
